statements.quote: The frontend for CueTip (See Fig. 9) was built using React[3] . We used the call frame from Daily.js[4] , which provides a real-time speech transcription service. The system was deployed using a website hosted on GitHub[5] . We used the GPT-4o-mini[6] model provided by OpenAI[7] . We built a React app with multiple routes: one for users to join the conversation and one for facilitators to control the meeting. To ensure synchronization of cue delivery, we used a Firebase Database[8] . We also used Generative AI to diagnose any errors in the system and analysis scripts.
statements.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 300), Sec. 3.3 (implementation and analysis scripts); markdown line 159

statements.quote: The raw notes from each session were reviewed by a research team member to check for duplicates and remove them. If there was any uncertainty about what counts as an individual idea, the team member would discuss with another team member and make a call. Notes from each session were assigned to research team members to ￿ll in any missing ideas by using the recording and the transcript of each session for reference. The number of ideas is then calculated by the number of points in each classi￿ed note.
statements.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 4.1.4, Number of Ideas (notes and recordings); markdown line 219

statements.quote: We pooled the ideas across all groups and ￿t a BERTopic [42] model to measure topic diversity. Since we did not have a pre-set number of topics, we used HDBSCAN for clustering, with the minimum cluster size as 15. We used the default con￿guration with the minimum cluster size on BERTopic documentation[10] . We used Shannon’s Entropy[11] from scipy[121] to calculate each idea’s topic diversity score.
statements.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 4.1.4, Topical Diversity of Generated Ideas (analysis software); markdown line 221

statements.quote: We transcribed all conversation audio ￿les collected using Assembly AI[12] . We then mapped the utterances from the ideation conversation transcript to all 698 Interactive Advertising Bureau[13] (IAB) topics and calculated the topic diversity using Assembly AI. Each IAB topic[14] is de￿ned by three hierarchical levels: a broad category (Level 1), a sub-category (Level 2), and a speci￿c topic (Level 3). For all words spoken by the same person in each round of conversation within each group, we measured the number of unique Level 1 topics covered. We then used the combined set of unique Level 1 topics from all rounds as the ￿nal score for the conversation’s topic diversity.
statements.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 4.1.4, Topic Diversity of Conversation from Transcripts; markdown line 223

statements.quote: Participants were provided links to the poststudy survey that was hosted on Qualtrics. We analyzed the data using JMP Pro, Google Sheets, and custom-built JavaScript analysis ￿les.
statements.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 4.1.4, Post Study Survey (software and custom scripts); markdown line 225

statements.quote: The audio comes from a total of 70 sessions, out of which 4 sessions were excluded from conversation analysis due to prominent echos, preventing us from automatically extracting insights using the Assembly AI service. Sixteen recordings were not included in the analysis as the screen recorder only recorded the researcher’s utterances and not those of the participants. We also performed a sanity check on ￿ve audio ￿les and found an accuracy of around 95%. We did not perform any post-processing on the transcripts obtained from Assembly AI
statements.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), footnote 12 (audio and transcript exclusions); markdown line 231

statements.quote: We had the recordings of each session, and the transcript from each ideation conversation with details regarding the utterances, timings and the same for the cue contents and their timings. Two members from the research team reviewed the transcripts and marked ‘Y’ or ‘N’ if the participants either explicitly mentioned the cue or read the cue out aloud, which would be marked as a ‘Y’. If not, they would be marked as a ‘N’. Two researchers coded a total of 41 session transcripts together. Due to a strong intercoder agreement, the rest of the transcripts were coded by one of the two research team members. Two sessions were excluded from this because of poor readability of transcripts due to echoes in the audio ￿le.
statements.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 4.1.4, Noticing Rate of Conversational Cues (recordings and coding); markdown line 237

notes.unit_and_arm_linkage: Session identifies a dyad. cue takes 'cue'/'no cue'; modality takes 'virtual'/'inperson'. Survey IDs have the form S<number>P1 or S<number>P2. All 171 survey rows join to Session in the idea table, with no cue-arm conflict. Conversation IDs also join without arm conflicts. Survey cue assignment is additionally indicated by the CSV filenames.
notes.participant_id_cautions: The 171 survey rows contain 169 distinct recorded IDs. S22P1 appears twice in NoCue and S67P1 twice in Cue, with different responses. S6P1, S22P2 and S67P2 have no row under those IDs. Do not silently relabel or deduplicate records or infer that the row count is an analyzed participant count.
notes.analysis_count_cautions: Idea quantity and idea-topic diversity each have 84 observed dyad scores; S5 and S15 are missing. Requiring dsgn and know leaves 72 dyads with outcomes. Conversation diversity has 66 observed scores and 55 complete cases with both covariates. These are availability/complete-case counts, not verified final REML sample sizes. No analysis scripts or exclusion flags fully reconcile the PDF's session-exclusion narrative.
notes.readme_idea_score_definition: Topic diversity: The topic diversity score is derived by calculating the entropy of topics from the  ideas generated by the dyad using Shannon's entropy
notes.readme_conversation_score_definition: Topic diversity: The topic diversity score is derived from the combined set of unique Level 1 (IAB topics) from all conversation turns

final.open_items[2]: The README defines idea-topic diversity as Shannon entropy of topics from ideas generated by the dyad. This confirms a dyad score and helps resolve the paper's per-idea/per-dyad wording; original topic allocations and implementation cannot be verified without texts or code.

Participant-level self-report means, SDs, SEs and response counts can be computed after resolving duplicate IDs and outcome-specific missingness. These are not the form's scored creative-output outcomes.

notes.source_read: Entire 1,080-line markdown, including references, acknowledgments and Appendices A.1-A.6. PDF pp. 15-17 additionally extracted with PyMuPDF; PDF hyperlinks verified the full OSF URL. PDF p. 1 is a cover sheet; printed page = PDF page + 295.
notes.quotation_policy: Quotes are copied from the supplied markdown (formatting removed from quoted headings) or the indicated PDF extraction. Missing-glyph characters already present in the sources are preserved. Spaces splitting the Appendix A.1 URL are source line-wrap artifacts; deposits.url uses the exact PDF hyperlink target.
notes.availability_scope: One explicit data-deposit statement: Appendix A.1. No preregistration, access-on-request, embargo or additional study-specific repository statement found. Acknowledgments contain no data/code statement. Embedded task instructions, prompts and questionnaires are materials, not additional deposits.
notes.status_basis: Participant survey responses, arm assignments (file identity and verified session-ID join), and numeric outcomes were read without credentials. The deposit also contains the randomized study's dyad-level scored outcomes. public_participant_data does not imply that individual creative outputs or every outcome are available.
notes.limitations: Idea quantity and idea/conversation diversity scores belong to dyads, not separately scored individuals. No raw idea texts, transcripts, audio, cue text, embeddings, per-idea distances, code, final analysis flags or randomization log found. S1-O4 and S2 are absent. The 171 survey rows are not 171 distinct recorded people.
notes.search_scope: All four requested APIs were searched by title and first author. Only the OSF project already named in the paper was relevant. OSF contributor discovery used full-name users search followed by public projects. Broad surname queries were narrowed. Identical repeated requests are consolidated; failed Zenodo size=100 requests and successful size=25 retries are separate.
